extraction_rationale: This is an enumerated land-use efficiency sub-action that reduces pressure on natural forests and supports the net-sink target.

policy_statement: Ban conversion of forested productive production forest to other land uses under Government Regulation No. 104/2015, with limited exceptions.
source_quote: To  avoid  further  conversion  of  forest,  Indonesia  has  issued  a  number  of regulations. Some of key regulations are: 1. Government Regulation No.104/2015 on the changes of forest land use and  function,  which  ban  the  conversion  of  forested  land  (productive production forest) in forest area for APL, except in the province where the non-forested lands in the production forest are not available; 2020
extraction_rationale: This is a binding regulatory mechanism to avoid forest conversion and land-use emissions.

policy_statement: Expand forest area protected for ecosystem-service value from 51.8 Mha to 65.3 Mha in the RPJMN 2020-2024.
source_quote: In  the  National  Medium-Term  Development  Plan  (RPJMN)  2020-2024,  forest area that need to be protected based on the value of ecosystem services of the forest, are expanded from 51.8 Mha to 65.3 Mha, which are located inside and outside forest area. This has to be considered in the process of developing land use planning at sub-national level.
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified protected-forest expansion target with a land-use planning link.

policy_statement: Limit cumulative future deforestation to 6.8 Mha under the LCCP pathway.
source_quote: The CPOS and LCCP indicate that expected cumulative area to be deforested in the future are about 14.6 Mha and 6.8 Mha respectively (see Figure 7). LCCP which requires future deforestation to be limited to 6.8 Mha to bring this sector becoming net sink also faces some challenges.
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified deforestation limit under the low-carbon pathway.

policy_statement: Require mandatory certification to promote sustainable production-forest management and achieve sustainable harvesting practices by all forest concession companies by 2050 under LCCP.
source_quote: Indonesia  has  issued mandatory  certification  systems  (Ministerial  Regulation  No.  30/  2016  by  the Minister of Environment and Forestry) that push the adoption of sustainable management practices in the production forests. With this policy, many forest concessions  have  improved  their  management  practices. Under  LCCP,  by 2050 all forest concession companies have implement sustainable harvesting practices.
section_header: b. Conservation and Sustainable Forest Management
extraction_rationale: This combines a binding certification mechanism with a dated universal implementation target for forest concessions.

policy_statement: Increase enhanced natural regeneration and forest restoration in production forests to about 1.70 Mha after 2030 and 8.8 Mha by 2050 under LCCP.
source_quote: Efforts  to  restore  the degraded production forest through enhanced natural regeneration (ENR) or forest restoration will also be increased. It is expected that under LCCP, area of production forest that being restored through the ENR programme after 2030 should reach about 1.70 Mha, about 2 times of the CPOS, and by 2050 it will reach 8.8 Mha or about 6 times of the CPOS.
section_header: b. Conservation and Sustainable Forest Management
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified ecosystem restoration target with dates and area values.

policy_statement: Protect peatland and prohibit new permits for peatland use under Presidential Instruction No. 5/2019.
source_quote: Significant amount of greenhouse gas emissions has been released from the use of peatland through decomposition and peat fire. At present emission from these sources contribute to about 50% of the total emission from AFOLU sector. Indonesia has issued a number of key policies to protect peatland and improve its management. Under Presidential Instruction No. 5/2019, there will not be any new permit for the use of peatland.
section_header: c. Protection and Restoration of Peatland
extraction_rationale: This is a binding permit prohibition for peatland protection, directly addressing peat decomposition and fire emissions.

policy_statement: Improve peatland and water management to 0.95 Mha by 2030 and 1.04 Mha by 2050 under LCCP.
source_quote: In addition, the Ministerial Regulation No. 15/2017 (Minister for Environment and Forestry) mandates private sector and local governments to improve the use of peatland and water management. Under  CPOS,  it  is  expected  that  the  improvement  of  peatland  and  water management by 2030 and 2050 reaches 0.86 Mha and 1.04 Mha consecutively, while under LCCP it should reach 0.95 Mha by 2030 and 1.04 Mha by 2050.
section_header: c. Protection and Restoration of Peatland
extraction_rationale: This policy has a binding ministerial regulation and quantified peatland/water-management targets under LCCP.

policy_statement: Increase degraded peatland restoration under LCCP to 2.7 Mha by 2030 and 4.2 Mha by 2050.
source_quote: For peatland restoration, CPOS figures the area of degraded peatland being restored should reach 1.03 Mha by 2030 and 1.7 Mha by 2050. While under LCCP, the target will be increased to 2.7 Mha by 2030 and 4.2 Mha by 2050.
section_header: c. Protection and Restoration of Peatland
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified ecosystem restoration target with 2030 and 2050 dates.

policy_statement: Accelerate afforestation, reforestation of degraded land, and urban revegetation to increase carbon sinks.
source_quote: Indonesia  will  accelerate  afforestation  and  reforestation  of  degraded  land inside and outside forest area as well as urban revegetation for increasing sink. At present many lands inside and outside forest areas are unproductive lands (Table 1). These lands are in the form of shrubs, grassland, and bare-lands.
extraction_rationale: This is a named biological carbon-sink enhancement intervention covering afforestation, reforestation and revegetation.

policy_statement: Implement agriculture-sector mitigation through low-emission rice varieties, water-saving paddy cultivation, livestock waste use for biogas, livestock feed improvement, and reduced synthetic fertilizer use.
source_quote: The effort to reduce emissions in  agriculture sector is emphasizing the presence of support on technology, finance and capacity development. The mitigation technologies accounted for in this sector are the adoption of low  emission  variety  and  water-saving  paddy  cultivation  system  (hereinafter referred to as SPR/STT) in the rice field, and utilization of livestock waste for biogas  and  livestock  feed  improvement  in  livestock  management,  and  the reduction in using synthetic fertilizer.
extraction_rationale: This is an umbrella agriculture mitigation package with a list of specific technologies and practices. It is treated as a parent because distinct sub-actions are described under rice field, livestock and fertilizer headings.

parent_statement: Agriculture-sector mitigation technologies and practices
policy_statement: Adopt low-emission rice varieties and water-saving paddy cultivation systems for rice fields.
source_quote: Mitigation activities in the rice field are referring to the type of land system 4 . For the paddy field with continuous flooding, the mitigation action is to implement a low emission variety, while for the paddy field with proper water management, SPR/STT is the feasible option. Emission factors for paddy fields in Indonesia are varied, from a high emitted variety (e.g. Inpari and Cisadane) to a low emitted variety (e.g. Dodokan).
extraction_rationale: This is a specific agricultural mitigation intervention for rice methane emissions and water use.

policy_statement: Adopt low-emission rice varieties on 0.97 Mha by 2030 and 2.07 Mha by 2050 under LCCP, covering about 24% of rice-field area by 2050.
source_quote: Under CPOS, the adoption of low emission variety is expected to be 0.93 Mha by 2030 and 1.96 Mha by 2050. Under LCCP, an ambitious target is set to 0.97 Mha by 2030 and 2.07 Mha by 2050.  The  adoption  scale  approximately  reaches  24%  of  the  total  rice  field area by 2050.
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified adoption target for a named low-emission agricultural technology.

parent_statement: Agriculture-sector mitigation technologies and practices
policy_statement: Use livestock waste for biogas and improve livestock feed supplements to reduce livestock emissions.
source_quote: The mitigation actions comprise the utilization of livestock waste for biogas and improvement of livestock feed supplement. The CPOS and LCCP are setting a similar target for biogas implementation, accounted for 41,000 head in 2030 and 94,000 head in 2050.
extraction_rationale: This is a named livestock mitigation action with a quantified biogas implementation target.

policy_statement: Apply improved livestock feed supplements to 6.58 million head by 2050 under LCCP to reduce methane from enteric fermentation.
source_quote: Research finds that shifting from high concentrate livestock feed to greenery feed,  specifically  in  beef  and  dairy  cattle,  is  potentially  reduce  methane emission from enteric fermentation. The feed supplement is a combination of the greenery and an additional feed supply of tannin from legume crops or urea molasses block. The target in CPOS and LCCP scenarios in 2050 is 3.42 million head and 6.58 million head, respectively.
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified livestock feed mitigation target tied to methane reduction.

parent_statement: Agriculture-sector mitigation technologies and practices
policy_statement: Encourage organic fertilizer substitution for urea to reduce dependence on nitrogen fertilizer use.
source_quote: Applying  organic  fertilizer  is  expected  to  reduce  dependency  on  nitrogen fertilizer  usage. Cropland  farmers  are  encouraged  to  use  organic  fertilizer to substitute the urea application. Under the assumed rate, urea dose under CPOS will be reduced from 0.1183 ton/ha in 2010 to 0.1174 ton/ha in 2050, while under LCCP will be reduced to 0.1172 ton/ha.
extraction_rationale: This is a named fertilizer-use intervention that reduces synthetic nitrogen use and associated emissions.

policy_statement: Adopt transformation policies to enhance crop productivity under LCCP, including improved technologies and practices, financial access, and labour productivity.
source_quote: Enhancing crop productivity under LCCP will need transformation policies that facilitates and increases the adoption of improved technologies and practices, improved  policy  for  financial  access  and  labour  productivity. The  following sections described transformation policies:
section_header: a. Improvement of Crop Productivity and Cropping Intensity
extraction_rationale: The passage explicitly introduces transformation policies and then lists subsections for technology, finance and labour productivity, so it is a parent policy.

parent_statement: Transformation policies to enhance crop productivity under LCCP
policy_statement: Support agricultural technology and machinery adoption to increase productivity and reduce post-harvest losses.
source_quote: Agricultural machinery support to farmers is the key to increase productivity to answer the challenges of increasing food demand in the future. There has been significant development of agricultural machinery support for farmers. Growth of  pre-harvest  machines  distribution  is  92%  during  2011-2019  in  the  form  of tractors, water pumps, transplants, cultivators, and sprayers aims to increase productivity.
extraction_rationale: This is a concrete technology-support intervention to increase agricultural productivity and reduce land-use pressure. Climate relevance is indirect because the immediate policy object is agricultural productivity.

parent_statement: Transformation policies to enhance crop productivity under LCCP
policy_statement: Increase farmer and farmer-group access to bank or non-bank financial institution credits for agricultural machinery and technology adoption.
source_quote: Under LCCP, technology adoption is assumed to be much higher due to an increase of farmers/farmers group access to credits from bank or NBFIs to purchase agricultural machinery based on their needs. Empowerment  of  farmers  group  and  innovative  agriculture  credit  schemes (individual or group lending) is a key to higher adoption technology in the future.
extraction_rationale: This is a credit-access policy supporting technology adoption for low-carbon agriculture. It is a financial instrument because it involves credits and lending schemes.

parent_statement: Transformation policies to enhance crop productivity under LCCP
policy_statement: Develop innovative agricultural value-chain finance schemes and optimise the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion to increase financing for low-carbon agriculture.
source_quote: The  development  of  innovative  schemes  in  agriculture  value  finance  is needed to increase access to capital from all actors along the chain (farmers, input traders and collectors/traders) to increase productivity of commodities. Under CPOS, value chain finance such as Warehouse receipt system, Peer to Peer lending (P2P) and credit programme provide credits to buy agricultural inputs and tools for technology adoption to support low carbon agriculture.
extraction_rationale: This is a financial-access policy using credit, value-chain finance and inclusion instruments to support low-carbon agriculture.

parent_statement: Transformation policies to enhance crop productivity under LCCP
policy_statement: Improve agricultural human-resource quality and capacity to support sustainable agriculture and low-carbon development.
source_quote: Improvement of quality and capacity of human resource in agriculture sector is  needed  to  support  sustainable  agriculture. Increase  of  human  resource capacity  correlate  with  higher  ability  and  skills  to  adopt  new  technology  to increase agricultural productivity. It will also increase the ability of farmers to play active role in the low carbon development process.
extraction_rationale: This is a capacity-building intervention tied to sustainable agriculture and low-carbon development. It is enabling rather than directly technical.

policy_statement: Use the Social Forestry Programme and TORA agrarian reform to grant legal access and land rights for agroforestry and improved farming in forest areas.
source_quote: By granting legal access through Social Forestry Programme, the farmers are eligible to receive supports from the government for the improvement of the farming activities by integrating the agriculture commodities with forest trees as agroforestry. Indonesia considers the Social Forestry Programme is a part of key solutions for addressing tenure issues and providing more access for community  to  utilise  forest  area and reducing poverty.
section_header: a. Improvement of Crop Productivity and Cropping Intensity
extraction_rationale: This is a named land-access and agroforestry policy. Climate relevance is indirect because tenure and poverty goals are also central.

policy_statement: Reduce food loss from 71 kg per capita in 2010 to 34 kg per capita by 2050 under LCCP through improved harvesting, cold storage and packaging.
source_quote: Modernization of harvesting tools is needed to improve harvesting techniques and reduce yield losses. Furthermore, assistance with cold storage facilities  and  packaging technology are essential to reduce food loss during food distribution. Improvements  in  harvest  and  post-harvest  technology  are expected to reduce food loss from 71 Kg per capita in 2010 to 40 Kg per capita in 2050 under CPOS and to 34 Kg per capita under LCCP.
section_header: d. Reducing Food Loss and Food Waste
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified resource-efficiency target with named technological interventions.

policy_statement: Implement a long-term low-carbon energy strategy based on energy efficiency, decarbonized electricity, fuel switching, and renewable-energy expansion.
source_quote: Four  following  guiding  pillars  were  used  to  develop  long-term  low  carbon strategy  in  energy  sector  taking  into account  past  development  and  future projection  of  energy  demand  and  supply  :  (i)  implementation  of  energy eff.shorticiency  measures;  (ii)  use  of  decarbonized  electricity  in  transport  and buildings; (iii) fuel shift from coal to gas and renewables in industry; and (iv) enhancement of renewable energy in power, transport and industry. Energy demand will increase along with economic development and population growth.

policy_statement: Nearly decarbonize the power sector by 2050 through massive renewables, CCS/CCUS on most coal power plants, and BECCS.
source_quote: It is expected that in 2050 the power sector will nearly decarbonised, through: (i) utilization of renewables (hydro, geothermal, solar, wind, biomass) in massive scale; (ii) most coal powerplants are equipped with CCS/CCUS; and (iii) biomass-coal cofiring power plants are connected to CCS (Biomass Energy with Carbon Capture and Storage or BECCS). Since Indonesia is an archipelago, the power system will be developed in the form of distributed power, instead of large centralised system.
extraction_rationale: This is a dated power-sector decarbonization commitment with named technologies.

policy_statement: Under the 2050 LCCP power mix, achieve 43% renewables, 38% coal, 10% natural gas, 8% BECCS, and equip around 76% of coal power plants with CCS.
source_quote: - Power generation mix are: renewables (43%), coal (38%), natural gas (10%) and BECCS (8%). - The renewables include hydro, geothermal, solar PV, biomass, biofuel and wind. - Around 76% of the coal power plant are equipped with CCS to achieve zero emissions in coal power plants.
extraction_rationale: This provides quantified power-generation mix and CCS deployment targets for 2050.

policy_statement: Develop 2050 renewable power installed capacity including 113 GW solar PV, 68 GW hydro, 23 GW geothermal, 17 GW wind, 13 GW biomass, 14 GW biofuel, and 23 GW BECCS.
source_quote: - Installed capacity of renewable power generation mix are: solar PV 113 GW, hydro 68 GW, geothermal 23 GW, wind power 17 GW, biomass 13 GW, biofuel 14 GW and BECCS 23 GW with negative emissions. - The supply availability of some renewable power plants are intermittent, and therefore, in order to have a reliable supply system it will require integration with continuous stable power supply system (baseload) such as coal power plants.
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified renewable and BECCS installed-capacity pathway.

policy_statement: Develop smart grids, off-grid, micro-grid, and 100% renewable smart microgrids for remote areas to manage intermittent renewable electricity.
source_quote: - Increasing development of 'off-grid' and 'micro-grid'. - Due to significant portion of intermittent renewable (solar and wind) will be deployed in the future, it will require development of smart grid that can handle large supply intermittency. - Power plant with 100% renewable energy in remote areas will need Smart Micro Grid.
extraction_rationale: This is a concrete grid-infrastructure intervention enabling high renewable penetration.

policy_statement: Achieve transport-sector mitigation through transport electrification, more biofuels for diesel substitution, and gasoline substitutes including bioethanol and CPO-based gasoline.
source_quote: The main energy source for transport are biofuels, oil fuels and electricity. Mitigation target in transport will be achieved by: (i) electrification of transport; (ii) supplying more biofuels for diesel substitute (fatty acid methyl-esther and bio-hydrocarbon or green diesel); and (iii) gasoline substitute (bioethanol and CPO-based gasoline). Since the past 10 years the government has introduce biofuels made from CPO, which is blended with petroleum diesel and called B20 (20% biodiesel plus 80% petroleum diesel).
extraction_rationale: This is a transport mitigation strategy with specific fuel-switching and electrification interventions.

policy_statement: Continue the biofuel programme to 2050 with higher biodiesel proportions including B30, B40 and B50 from sustainable sources.
source_quote: - The breakdown of transport energy in 2050 are: biofuels (46%), oil fuels (20%), electricity (30%) and natural gas (4%). The biofuel (CPO-based) programme is considered successful and will be continued to 2050 by supplying biofuel with higher biodiesel proportions (B30, B40, B50), which will be produced from sustainable sources.
extraction_rationale: This is a dated biofuel programme continuation with quantified 2050 energy shares and named blending levels.

policy_statement: Deploy CCS and CCUS at large scale under LCCP to reduce energy-sector emissions after 2030 toward around 572 Mton CO2e in 2050.
source_quote: The LCCP will give the lowest emission level in 2050, where high impact mitigation actions such as carbon capture and storage (CCS) as well as carbon capture, utilization and storage  (CCUS)  will  be  largely implemented. Under  the LCCP, a significant decreasing trend of emissions will occur after 2030 from 1,030 Mton CO 2 e towards around 572 Mton CO 2 e in 2050.
extraction_rationale: This identifies specific mitigation technologies and a quantified sectoral emissions pathway.

policy_statement: Reduce waste-sector GHG emissions under LCCP so emissions decline after 2030 and reach 120 Mton CO2e in 2050.
source_quote: The long-term pathway considers both historical development and projection of future waste management activities (reduction, avoidance, destruction, and utilization of GHG emissions), particularly methane gas (CH 4 ) from the waste treatment processes of municipal solid waste (MSW), domestic wastewater, and industrial waste. Under  LCCP, GHG emissions level will decrease after 2030 and reach 120 Mton CO 2 e in 2050.
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified waste-sector emissions target with named waste-management mechanisms.

source_quote: The long-term pathway considers both historical development and projection of future waste management activities (reduction, avoidance, destruction, and utilization of GHG emissions), particularly methane gas (CH 4 ) from the waste treatment processes of municipal solid waste (MSW), domestic wastewater, and industrial waste. The projection of GHG emissions assumed the rate of increase in the amount of waste generation and waste to be treated in each treatment unit is affected by population, economic growth, policies and regulations, lifestyle, treatment plans, and the success of source reduction activities.

policy_statement: Require local governments to manage municipal solid waste under Law No. 18/2008 and use Jakstranas, Jakstrada and Presidential Regulation No. 35/2018 to support GHG reduction through PLTSa or RDF.
source_quote: Law No. 18/2008 regarding MSW management obliges local governments to manage MSW. In addition, there are National Policy and Strategy (Jakstranas) and Provincial Policy and Strategy (Jakstrada) in waste management as well as Presidential Regulation No. 35/2018 concerning MSW utilization for electricity generation in PLTSa or RDF (refuse-derived fuels) that support GHG emission reduction.
extraction_rationale: This combines a binding MSW management law with named waste-to-energy regulations that support emissions reduction.

policy_statement: Under CPOS, manage municipal solid waste through 30% source reduction by 3R and 70% treatment through landfilling, composting and waste-to-energy.
source_quote: Currently, most of MSW is transported to SWDS after it is reduced at sources, composted, recycled, and recovered. Under CPOS, the MSW will be managed through waste reduction at sources (30%) by 3R (reduce-reuse-recycle) and waste treatment (70%) through landfilling, composting, and converting waste to energy. This 3R is a part of Circular Economy which is promoted in Indonesia.
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified waste-management strategy with specified treatment and circular-economy mechanisms.

policy_statement: Under LCCP, expand landfill gas recovery, PLTSa/RDF/SRF, biodigesters, paper recycling, composting, septic tank use for all new houses, and waste-to-energy.
source_quote: LCCP increases the potential of TRNS and CPOS mitigation significant adding the number of SWDS equipped with LFG recovery, the amount of MSW used for PLTSa and RDF/SRF, the number of biodigester equipped with biogas and sludge recovery, and the number of paper recycling and composting. The mitigation also covers the increase of septic tanks utilisation (100% new houses) equipped with biogas recovery or aerobic, sludge recovery systems and increased utilization of waste for energy.
extraction_rationale: This is a specific LCCP waste-sector technology package with a quantified 100% new-house septic-tank component.

policy_statement: Extend and increase IPPU mitigation policies through blended cement, advanced ammonia plant technology, N2O destruction, lower-PFC aluminium technology, and low-carbon iron and steel production.
source_quote: In the long-term mitigation scenarios, the CPOS assumed that mitigation and policies under unconditional NDC are extended to 2050 through cement blended and improving ammonia plants with advanced technology. The TRNS assumed mitigation potentials of unconditional NDC will be increased by adding more mitigation actions such as : (i) installing N 2 O emissions destruction in nitric acid industries, (ii) using lower PFCs (CF 4 /C 2 F 6 )  emissions technology in aluminium productions, and (iii) utilizing scrap and low carbon emitting technology in iron and steel production.
extraction_rationale: This is an umbrella IPPU mitigation package with explicitly listed technologies and sectors, including 2050 extension of NDC policies.

policy_statement: Reduce the impact of climate change on national GDP loss by 3.45% in 2050 by increasing resilience in food, water, energy and environmental health.
source_quote: By extending adaptation strategy in Updated NDC, the adaptation pathways set the goal to reduce the impact of climate change on national GDP loss by 3.45% in 2050, through increasing resilience in four basic necessities (food, water, energy, and environmental health), with three target areas of resilience (economy, social and livelihood, ecosystem and landscape). The economic resilience is manifested in the form of long-term investments based on risk codes such as climate hotspots, climate vulnerability, sectoral and regional-based adaptive development.
extraction_rationale: This is a quantified national adaptation target with a 2050 date and defined resilience domains.

policy_statement: Use long-term investments based on risk codes, climate hotspots, climate vulnerability and sectoral and regional adaptive development to build economic resilience.
source_quote: The economic resilience is manifested in the form of long-term investments based on risk codes such as climate hotspots, climate vulnerability, sectoral and regional-based adaptive development. Equally, the social and livelihoods resilience  is  translated  into  enhancement  of  human  resource  capacity  and creation of green job opportunities.
extraction_rationale: This identifies a specific climate-risk investment-planning mechanism for adaptation.

policy_statement: Build social and livelihood resilience through human-resource capacity enhancement and green job creation.
source_quote: The economic resilience is manifested in the form of long-term investments based on risk codes such as climate hotspots, climate vulnerability, sectoral and regional-based adaptive development. Equally, the social and livelihoods resilience  is  translated  into  enhancement  of  human  resource  capacity  and creation of green job opportunities.
extraction_rationale: This is a resilience-building intervention for people and livelihoods. It is less technically specific than infrastructure actions, but explicitly framed as climate resilience.

policy_statement: Build ecosystem and landscape resilience through sustainable landscape management, integrated terrestrial and marine ecosystem management, and conservation.
source_quote: Equally, the social and livelihoods resilience  is  translated  into  enhancement  of  human  resource  capacity  and creation of green job opportunities. Likewise, the ecosystem and landscape resilience are directed towards sustainable landscape management through integrated terrestrial and marine ecosystem management and conservation.
extraction_rationale: This uses ecosystem management and conservation as the mechanism for climate resilience.

policy_statement: Implement regional and sectoral adaptation pathways based on basic necessities including food, water, energy and environmental health.
source_quote: Regional and sectoral approaches were used in developing  climate  resilient  pathways.  The Regional Pathway focuses on priority areas to implement adaptation  actions  based  on  several  basic  necessities (food, water, energy, and environmental health), taking consideration  the  following  aspects:  climate,  climate sensitive,  non-climate  sensitive,  and  social  economy. Adaptation  actions  under  the  Sectoral  Pathway  also based  on  the  same  basic  necessities  as  the  Regional Pathway.
extraction_rationale: This is a specific adaptation planning approach with named pathways, priority areas and resilience criteria.

policy_statement: Strengthen synergy between ministries and sectoral agencies as an enabling environment for implementing the long-term climate resilience strategy.
source_quote: Adaptation  actions  under  the  Sectoral  Pathway  also based  on  the  same  basic  necessities  as  the  Regional Pathway. Synergy between ministries/sectoral agencies as prerequisites for the successful of the implementation of the long-term strategy on climate resilience will be part of  the key enabling environments to be strengthened over time.
extraction_rationale: This is a governance implementation commitment for climate resilience.

policy_statement: Use SIDIK vulnerability index data and climate hotspots to identify priority regions for adaptation interventions.
source_quote: The priority regions are the most vulnerable to the negative impacts of climate change which  should  be  reviewed  on  a  regional  scale.  The  priority  regions can be analysed based on the vulnerability index data and climate hotspot. The vulnerability index (SIDIK) 9  is built by using flood and drought risk maps, socio-economic data, and environmental infrastructure.
extraction_rationale: This is a specific adaptation planning and targeting mechanism using named vulnerability and climate hotspot tools.

policy_statement: Translate NDC adaptation commitments into multi-sectoral adaptation action programs through the NDC Road Map strategy and indicators.
source_quote: Efforts to translate NDC commitments into adaptation actions are formulated through the NDC Road map strategy consisting of adaptation action pillars with indicators to see the results of adaptation activities. Furthermore, the pillars of the Road map strategy can become a direction for planning adaptation action programs contained in multi-sectoral actions which are used as input towards LTS-LCCR 2050 in the aspect of adaptation.
extraction_rationale: This is a concrete adaptation planning framework using the NDC Road Map, pillars, indicators and multi-sectoral programs.

policy_statement: Plan and implement sectoral adaptation based on basic necessities while avoiding maladaptation through inter-sectoral coordination.
source_quote: Planning and implementing adaptation in sectoral pathway must be conducted based  on  basic  necessities  (see  Figure  45).  It  is  also  important  to  avoid mal-adaptation that potentially occur if the adaptation is carried out without coordination  amongst  sectors.  The  synergy  between  sectoral  ministries/ agencies  is  needed  in  climate  change  adaptation.
extraction_rationale: This is a climate adaptation implementation requirement with a concrete coordination mechanism and maladaptation safeguard.

policy_statement: Continue strengthening community climate change actions through PROKLIM implementation in parallel with low-carbon lifestyle adoption.
source_quote: All  sectors  should  also consider cross-cutting issues, such as knowledge management sharing (i.e., increasing literacy) and community engagement for local climate actions. As a real example, Indonesia will continue to strengthen climate change actions of the community through PROKLIM implementation, in parallel with the adoption of low carbon lifestyle.
extraction_rationale: PROKLIM is a named community climate action program. The commitment is explicit, though operational detail is limited in this passage.

policy_statement: Use the estimated adaptation funding framework for roadmap governance and implementation, including IDR 12.84 trillion for roadmap governance.
source_quote: Funding needs for adaptation are divided into two parts, namely funding for road map governance (5% - 10%) and funding for adaptation implementation (90% - 95%). The first funding group is  more  towards  initiating,  managing,  coordinating,  reporting,  monitoring, and evaluating the proposed adaptation actions, and the second one is the estimated costs required to implement the adaptation actions. As for funding for the road map governance (i.e., enabling condition for the implementation  of  adaptation  actions),  the estimated total funding required is about IDR 12.84 trillion.
extraction_rationale: This provides a quantified adaptation finance framework and allocation categories. It is based on estimated funding needs rather than a fully appropriated budget, so it is somewhat less binding.

policy_statement: Japan examined and prepared the Plan for Global Warming Countermeasures as the comprehensive plan for implementing its 2030 emissions-reduction goal.
source_quote: At the joint meetings of the Mid- and Long-Term Climate Change Countermeasures Subcommittee of the Global Environment Committee under the Central Environment Council and the Working Group for Consideration of Global Warming Countermeasures of the Global Environment Subcommittee of the Committee on industrial Science and Technology Policy and Environment under the Industrial Structural Council, the examination was conducted on the Plan for Global Warming Countermeasures, a comprehensive plan for the implementation of Japan's emissions reduction goal for the year 2030, in a transparent manner to the public, while holding hearing from future generations and relevant ministries and agencies. With regard to energy policy and energy mix, the examination was conducted in a transparent manner to the public at the Advisory Committee for Natural Resources and Energy. Through the above procedures, the Government prepared a draft which was adopted by the Global Warming Prevention Headquarters.
extraction_rationale: The Plan for Global Warming Countermeasures is a named comprehensive implementation plan for the 2030 emissions-reduction goal. It qualifies as a planning policy tied to a quantified mitigation target.

policy_statement: Japan made net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 a Basic Principle of the Act on Promotion of Global Warming Countermeasures.
source_quote: Japan aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net-zero, that is, to realize carbon neutrality by 2050, based on the idea that addressing climate change is no longer a constraint on economic growth and that proactive climate change measures bring transformation of industrial structures as well as its economy and society, leading to dynamic economic growth. By the Act Partially Amending the Act on Promotion of Global Warming Countermeasures (Act No. 54 of 2021) which was enacted in 204th session of the Diet, net-zero by 2050 became a Basic Principle of the Act. The legislative amendment will enhance the continuity and predictability of policies and accelerate efforts and investments as well as innovation for decarbonization towards not only the achievement of the mid-term target, but also the realization of a decarbonized society.
extraction_rationale: This is a legally anchored national climate target: the 2050 net-zero objective became a Basic Principle of an amended Act. The statutory mechanism makes it a policy commitment.

policy_statement: Japan will pursue its fiscal year 2030 emissions target through thorough energy efficiency measures, maximum introduction of renewable energy, and decarbonization of public sectors and local communities.
source_quote: On top of that, Japan aims to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions by 46 percent in fiscal year 2030 from its fiscal year 2013 levels, setting an ambitious target which is aligned with the long- term goal of achieving net-zero by 2050. Furthermore, Japan will continue strenuous efforts in its challenge to meet the lofty goal of cutting its emissions by 50 percent. In order to create a virtuous cycle of the economy and the environment and to realize robust growth toward its ambitious goal for fiscal year 2030, Japan will put forward all possible efforts in all areas including by thorough energy efficiency measures, maximum introduction of renewable energy, as well as decarbonization of public sectors and local communities.
extraction_rationale: This is an implementation commitment tied to the quantified 2030 target and names specific intervention types: energy efficiency, renewable energy, and public/local decarbonization. Energy efficiency is explicitly named, so Resource Efficiency is assigned as a secondary category.

policy_statement: Japan will proceed with strategic transitions to a circular economy as part of its decarbonization pathway.
source_quote: Japan will create new industries and jobs by proceeding efforts in strategic transitions to a circular economy, which is necessary for decarbonization, as well as through nature-based solutions (NbS). Japan will continue its strenuous efforts towards 2030, and further towards 2050. Realizing carbon-neutrality by 2050 and cutting emissions by 46 percent in fiscal year 2030 is certainly not an easy task; it is therefore essential to position decarbonization as one of the main issues in all socio-economic activities and to bring forward the transformation into sustainable and resilient socio-economic systems.
extraction_rationale: This is a stated commitment to strategic circular-economy transitions and explicitly links them to decarbonization. The primary mechanism is resource optimization, and the quote also explicitly references carbon-neutrality and emissions cuts, so Mitigation is assigned as a secondary category.

policy_statement: Japan will establish and implement the Joint Crediting Mechanism to secure approximately 100 million t-CO2 of accumulated emission reductions and removals by fiscal year 2030 and count acquired credits toward its NDC.

By doing so, through public-private collaborations, Japan aims to secure accumulated emission reductions and removals at the level of approximately 100 million t-CO 2 by fiscal year 2030. Japan will appropriately count the acquired credits to achieve its NDC.

policy_statement: Increase the resilience of Kuwait's fisheries and marine sector to climate change.
source_quote: Climate change stressors are expected to affect the marine and fisheries sector: The potential risks threaten coral reef communities and other aquatic communities. The susceptibility of these invaluable ecosystems to climate change is increasing due to nonclimate change stressors. The coastal and marine ecosystems degradation is expected to multidirectional socio-economic outcomes: for instance, poor seawater quality would require sophisticated pretreatments that increase the coast water (Andrianne & Alardin, 2003). Thus, controlling these non-climate change stressors is a mandatory adaptation option to increase the resilience of this sector to climate change. Other adaptation options are initiating researches to assess the impact of spatial and temporal distributions of SST, salinity. pH and SDD on coastal and marine ecosystems and enhancing the existed coastal and marine monitoring systems by integrating remote sensing technologies.

policy_statement: Improve resilience of Kuwait's water systems through awareness, conservation technologies, risk assessment, tariff reform, efficient irrigation, improved water treatment, water-efficient devices, research, and climate-hydrological modelling.
source_quote: Climate change risks are expected to cause significant negative socio-economic outputs: Increased cost of water desalination and loss of farmers' income are the most potential socioeconomic outcomes. Thus, enhancing the resilience of systems for water supply and management is a mandatory adaptation step to minimize the impact of climate change on this sector. Increasing water block-tariff to control unnecessary water consumptions, reducing physical leakages, utilizing technologies to reduce water consumption, and adopting efficient irrigation methods to reduce water losses are shortterm adaptation options that can minimize the effects of climate change on this sector.

policy_statement: Enhance the resilience of coastal zones to sea-level-rise risks through vulnerability assessments, information access, capacity building, awareness, financial aid, legislation, coastal management institutions, protection barriers, and coastline protection policies.
source_quote: Inundation of low lying areas due to SLR will have a great influence on human settlements and terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems of the coastal zone. Damage of infrastructure and important facilities, saltwater intrusion, loss of terrestrial habitats, disturbance of coastal and marine ecosystems, increase in coastal erosion, decrease in water transparency due to increasing coastal erosion, and shoreline retreat are significant SLR hazards and impacts. Designing adaptive long-term coastal plans to restrict establishing major projects on vulnerable coasts is very urgent action that must be taken. to establish such adaptive plans, more researches assessing the impacts of SLR on the coastal zone of Kuwait are needed. Also, raising awareness among decision-makers in Kuwait to incorporate SLR scenarios into upcoming development plans is an important adaptation step. SLR risks are expected to disturb the coastal wildlife: An adaptation option to enhance the resilience of coastal wildlife is to legislate laws that restrict negative anthropogenic activities in the coastal zone.

policy_statement: Build the capacity of Kuwait's health sector to prepare for increased climate-related health risks, including dust events, heat waves, heavy rain, flash floods, and thunderstorms.
source_quote: Increasing dust events and heat waves are the most significant physical effects of climate change on the health sector. Dust events significantly contribute to degrading the air quality increasing risks of chronic diseases and deaths. Also, heat waves are expected to increase risks of injuries and deaths. The potential socio-economic outcomes of these risks are the loss of work capacity and productivity and an increase in the treatment cost of chronic diseases, such as asthma. Enhancing the building capacity of the health sector to be prepared for increased risks due to climate change must be set as an objective of climate change adaptation for this sector. Immediate adaptation actions should be taken to ensure the achievement of this objective. These adaptation actions include but not limited to initiating researches to investigate the risks of climate change induced diseases, adjusting the office working hours to avoid working during maximum temperature in the day, raising the awareness of how to respond to dust and heat waves events and establishing national health alerts for dust and heat wave events.
